en: Now begins the introductory rules (*paribhāṣā*) in the *Baudhāyana-gṛhyasūtra*. Now begins the first book (*praśna*).

Now it is indeed said: "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is born burdened with three debts: toward the seers by means of the life of a student (*brahmacarya*), toward the gods by means of sacrifice (*yajña*), and toward the ancestors by means of offspring (*prajā*). (1)

We shall now explain the life of sacred study (*brahmacarya*). From the time of initiation until the *samāvartana* ceremony, one becomes a student of sacred study only when he has fulfilled his vows; thus, that stage of life (*āśrama*) has been explained. Hereafter follows the life of sacred study by which one becomes free from debt.
"Only with one's own wife" is one [rule];
"with the application of the mantra" is another;
"during the fertile period" is yet another.
Now, regarding the rules for studentship (*adhibrahmacaryam*): [one must remain celibate] for three nights during a wedding;
(8) for three nights during the fertile period (*ṛtu*);
(9) and for one night after having given or eaten at a *śrāddha* ceremony on the new moon day or the full moon day. (10)
11. Also for a day with regard to the wives of others, and for as long as one lives.
12. For twelve nights during the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya).
13. For one night on the days of fasting (upavasatha) for the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, the iṣṭi sacrifices, and the animal sacrifices (paśubandha).
In the same way, [the rule applies] to all Vedic rituals (14);
to the Cāturmāsya sacrifices for a year (15);

and according to their specific application in other sacrificial rites (yajñakratu), except during the [specific] seasons, in long-term sacrificial sessions (dīrghasattra), and in the Gharma-vows (16).

Thus has been explained celibacy (*brahmacarya*), which is righteous, meritorious, conducive to offspring, conducive to long life, conducive to heaven, conducive to fame, and the discharge of debt. (17) With the words "By sacrifice to the gods," we shall now explain sacrifice (*yajña*). (18) Sacrifice consists of twenty-one forms; it is composed of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* [Vedas]; it is built up by the meters (*chandas*); it possesses domestic and wild animals, plants, and oblations (*havis*); and it is made enduring through sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). (19)

That [sacrifice] is to be known as fourfold: the sacrifice of study (*svādhyāya-yajña*), the sacrifice of recitation (*japa-yajña*), the sacrifice of ritual action (*karma-yajña*), and the mental sacrifice (*mānasa-yajña*).
(20) Among these, each subsequent one is ten times superior in vigor to the preceding one.
(21) This applies without distinction to each of the four stages of life: the student (*brahmacārin*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vanastha*), and the ascetic (*yati*). (22)

All these [rites] are indeed not prohibited for the householder, because they consist of action (kriyātmaka). 23. There is no Brāhmaṇa who is inactive; no twice-born man who lacks consecration (saṃskāra); no Vipra who is ignorant; and one devoid of these is not a Śrotriya; nor is there a sacrifice for one who is not a Śrotriya. 24. Therefore, conduct (ācāra) is the authority; conduct is the established order (saṃsthā), conduct is action, and conduct is continuity, because of the necessity of its constant presence. 25.

Therefore, anyone who performs actions and whose conduct is approved by the virtuous should be known as a *śrotriya* alone. 16. Moreover, they cite this: those twice-born men who have been duly consecrated with mantras during the rites of impregnation (*niṣeka*), the sacraments of the womb (*garbhasaṃskāra*), and the birth-rites (*jātakarma*), and who have completed their vows, are to be known as *śrotriyas*; and those who have mastered a branch of the Veda (*śākhāpāra*). When two such persons, having duly taken each other’s hand according to the *Gṛhya* rules and having fulfilled their vows, unite with mantras, they produce an embryo that possesses Brahminhood.
27. Therefore, conduct is the authority. 28.

Thus ends the first chapter of the first book in the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra*. Now begins the second chapter of the first book. Now, it is indeed said: "By means of the entire sacrifice, the gods went to the heavenly world. This entire sacrifice begins with the *huta* (the offering into the fire) and extends up to the *sahasrasaṃvatsara* (the thousand-year sacrifice). For whatever one knows regarding the rites of private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), recitation (*japa*), and mental meditation (*mānasa*), by that very quality of his, his sacrifice becomes accomplished. Thus, this *Mantra-brāhmaṇa* has been explained. 1.
Now, it is indeed said: "The gods, not finding prosperity, saw it in the couple. Having understood this, they took wives and became partakers of all sacrifices; thus the sacrifice has been explained.

[Regarding the phrase] "Through offspring [he pays his debt] to the ancestors": the offspring he produces, those whom he initiates, those whom he causes to study, and those for whom he performs sacrifices—all these constitute his offspring; thus offspring has been explained. "He who has a son, who is a sacrificer, and who has lived as a student of sacred knowledge—he is indeed free from debt. By this, he is said to be one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*).

Moreover, they cite this: "The word *pud* is a name for hell, and they know hell to be suffering. Because he protects (*trāṇa*) from that, one desires a son both in this world and in the next. A son who is merely a lump of flesh, nor one who is unlearned, nor even one who performs no rites, does not go to heaven himself; how much less could he deliver his father? (5) It is known [in the Veda]: "I am you, you are me; this is mine, you are my source, I am your source. Being mine indeed, O Jātavedas, carry the oblations forward as a son who creates the world for his father. (6)

Therefore, he is said to be free from debt toward the *gārhapatya*; from the *gārhapatya* comes the *āhavanīya*, therefore one is free from debt through the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) toward the *āhavanīya*. From the *āhavanīya* comes the fire brought forward (*praṇīta*), therefore one is free from debt as a performer of animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*). From the *śālāmukhīya* comes the *āgnīdhrīya*, and from the *āgnīdhrīya* come the other hearths (*dhiṣṇya*). (7) "Thou art pervasive, O carrier," with these [verses] one performs the ritual distribution and the worship; this constitutes his divine progeny, therefore one is free from debt as a performer of Soma sacrifices. (8) Therefore, all these sacrifices belong to the householder; therefore, the household life is superior. (9)
Now, regarding the attainment of his welfare during the "waxing fortnight," this refers specifically to the first half of the month; it is explained by means of the moon as it waxes.
(10) Or rather, days and nights are both increasing and decreasing. That period in which the days increase is what is meant here.
(11) Now, according to some, it is known that one should perform [the rite] at five times of the day; this is said to be equivalent to saying "during the northern course of the sun. (12)

A year is indeed a day and night for the gods; of that [year], the northern course of the sun is the day and the southern course is the night. One should perform [the rites] at five times of that day: at the morning and the *saṅgava* (forenoon) [one should perform] the cold season and spring; at midday, the summer; at the afternoon and the evening, the rainy season and autumn. They do not perform the marriage ceremony at the morning and the *saṅgava*, nor in the evening; however, one may perform the others at will. 13.

Now, regarding the statement "one should perform [the rite] at another auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*)," there are some lunar mansions belonging to the gods and others belonging to Yama. One should perform whatever rite one intends to do during those lunar mansions that belong to the gods; this is what is meant by that statement. Thus ends the second chapter of the first book in the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra*.
Now begins the third chapter of the first book.

Viṣṇu and Soma indeed engaged in a theological debate. Viṣṇu said, "I am the foundation of the Brāhmaṇas," while Soma said, "I am the foundation. They both approached Prajāpati with this question, and he, Prajāpati, replied: "The meters go to Viṣṇu, and the lunar mansions go to Soma; therefore, you two are both devoted to Brahman. He continued: "Being honored, honor [others]; being praised, praise [others]; being dear, remain dear; being devoted to Brahman, remain devoted to Brahman; being knowers of Brahman, remain knowers of Brahman; and be the establishers of the boon. 1.

"Whoever the Brahmins shall declare me to be at the sacrifices, that I shall be," so said Viṣṇu; therefore Viṣṇu is the sacrifice, for it is known that "the sacrifice is indeed the foundation of the Brahmins. And because it is known that "the Brahmins are indeed the meters," [he is established as such].

"Whoever the Brahmins shall declare me to be among the lunar mansions, that I shall be," so said Soma; therefore Soma is the king of the Brahmins, and thus it is known that "the Brahmin is indeed the twenty-eighth of the lunar mansions"—that is his meritorious word.
Both of them are devoted to Brahman, knowers of Brahman, the establishers of the Brāhmaṇas, and are themselves established among the Brāhmaṇas.

(4) He who, knowing this, performs rites preceded by Brāhmaṇas, does so for the success of the sacrifice. (5) By this [rule], the even and the uneven, the equal and the unequal, as well as the rites for the gods and the rites for the ancestors, are explained. (6)

One who is about to perform the Vedic rites, having first bathed at a sacred ford (tīrtha), emerged from the water, put on a fresh garment, sipped water (ācamana), and purified himself with twenty-one bunches of *darbha* grass, purifies the person for whom he is performing them. It is known from scripture: "The *darbha* grasses are indeed a purifier; Viṣṇu is the purifier; [this is] for the establishment of Soma. (7)

He purifies him with twenty-one [verses]. The sacrifice is twenty-onefold; man is twenty-onefold; there are twenty-one meters; there are twenty-one worlds of the gods. Having established the sacrificer upon the twenty-onefold [world] by means of the meters and the sacrifice, he purifies him as one who is purified, fit for sacrifice, and worthy of the altar. He purifies him with seven [verses]. There are seven meters; verily, by means of the meters he purifies him. He purifies him with seven [verses]; these seven persons of his extend their continuity along [the line], three facing forward and three facing backward.

"The self is the seventh; he purifies them by just this many. "He purifies with those divided threefold; these worlds are three; it is by means of these very worlds that he purifies him"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. 8.

Then, having sipped water and having become purified both externally and internally, pure, fit for sacrifice, and ready to perform the Vedic rites, one should feed an even number of Brāhmaṇas on the day before; these are said to be the Nāndīmukhas. 9.

When they have finished eating, at the place for the *svadhā* offering, he mutters this *yajus*: "I shall conceive honey; I shall be born as honey. Then he pours out water with the formula, "May the *nāndīmukha* ancestors be pleased. This is indeed what is called the *svadhā*. (20) They do not perform the ancestral (*pitrya*) and divine (*daiva*) rites on the same day. For him who performs the ancestral and divine rites on the same day, his offspring will be subject to early death. Therefore, it is performed for the ancestors on the preceding day. Regarding this, there is a *brāhmaṇa* passage: "Having thus ransomed the sacrifice from the ancestors, the sacrificer extends it further. (11)
Thus ends the third chapter of the first book in the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra.
Now begins the fourth chapter of the first book:
"Then, on the following day, [the sacrifice] for the gods," so it is said. 1.
Then, on the following day, one should serve food to the Brahmins; this constitutes the rite for the deity.

(2) Whatever deity it may be, when about to cause them to pronounce an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), he pronounces its name, saying, "May such-and-such [the deity] be pleased. (3) When about to cause them to pronounce an auspicious day, he honors the Brahmins. (4)
5. They stand facing the east in pairs with their hands not empty.
6. To their south, the reciter stands facing north, holding a covered water-pot. 7.
Another stands behind him, grasping his right arm.
Then he honors them with the words, "May the mind be concentrated.
"Our minds are concentrated," is the reply of the others.
The mind is indeed the moon, and the Brāhmaṇas are the lunar mansions; therefore, he concentrates the mind upon the Brāhmaṇas.
"May you be gracious," he says. "We are gracious," is the reply of the others.
In this very way they become gracious toward him.

"May there be peace; may there be nourishment; may there be contentment; may there be prosperity; may there be freedom from obstacles; may there be long life; may there be health; may the rite be auspicious"—with these words he invokes this very blessing.
In the same way, there is a response from the others: "Om" is Brahman; "Om" is this entire universe.

Therefore, having joined [the words] with "Om," [he says], "May you, sirs, declare it an auspicious day. By this, both the day and the lunar mansion become pure; they, being pure, purify him. (15) "Om, may you, sirs, pronounce blessings! By this, the benediction for cattle and Brahmins is expressed. They, indeed, fulfill him with that blessing. (16)
"May you, sirs, speak of prosperity (*ṛddhi*). By this, the prosperity of the *ṛg*, *yajus*, and *sāman* [Vedas] is declared; through these alone one becomes prosperous.
(17) He who, knowing thus, causes the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be made, his ritual act does not become impaired.

(18) Whatever ritual act he performs, the procedure is to move clockwise around the fire while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*); such rites are performed for the gods, while the opposite is done for the ancestors (*pitrya*). (19)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra.
Now begins the fifth chapter in the first book.
Regarding the statement, "In a pure and level place," how is this to be understood? 1.
A square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide is smeared with cow-dung; it thus becomes pure.

(2) Having dug out the center of that [mound] and sprinkled [it with water], he makes a square sacrificial mound one cubit (*aratni*) on each side. Therein, he proceeds with the ritual acts beginning with the drawing of lines.
(3) To the south, upon *darbha* grass, a Brāhmaṇa sits down. If he sits down, he prays while lifting up his face toward the quarters. (4)

If, however, he does not sit down, he places a *kūrca* (seat-grass mat) on the south side with its tips pointing eastward upon the *darbha* grass, and worships [the Brahman] with: "Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ oṃ; O Brahman, you are the Brahman; homage to you, the Brahman. Thus, the Brahman himself becomes seated there. He grants him a boon, or he should feed a Brāhmaṇa. (5) By this, the sacrifice is complete with its head.
For whoever knows the head of the sacrifice becomes possessed of a head and fit for sacrifice. (6)

To the north [he places] a water-pot, a Brāhmaṇa, the fuel, and the sacrificial grass; for it is said in the Brāhmaṇa: "The head of the sacrifice is indeed this; he who knows thus becomes possessed of a head and fit for the sacrifice. (7) Then he lays down the *śamyā*-sticks as enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), for it is known: "The *śamyās* are indeed the enclosing-sticks. One should not offer an oblation without having laid down the enclosing-sticks, for the purpose of warding off the *rakṣases*. (8) In every case, the teachers maintain that there should be sweeping around, sprinkling, strewing, laying down the enclosing-sticks, adding fuel, and adorning, out of respect for the ritual requirements. (9)

Having adorned everything everywhere and having obtained the permission of the Brahmins who are present there, he should perform whatever he intends to do; that which he performs will indeed be successful for him.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaparibhāṣā-sūtra.
Now begins the sixth chapter in the first book.

"In all *darvihoma* offerings that include the *āghāra* libations, one recites the *puronuvākyā* and then offers the oblation with the *yājyā* for the sake of providing a deity," so says the Brāhmaṇa. (1) Where a single [verse] is prescribed, one should repeat it twice. (2) Having recited "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ... (*tatsaviturvareṇyam*), one offers the oblation over the prescribed [verse]. Alternatively, having recited "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ om," one offers the oblation with "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ... (*tatsaviturvareṇyam*). (3)

In cases where no specific rule has been prescribed, this general expiation applies. (4) Regarding oblations to Viṣ� cooked offerings should be made for the rites of naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first outing (*upaniṣkrāmaṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the commencement of Vedic study (*upākarma*), and the observances (*vrata*); there are no uncooked offerings in these *pākayajñas*. In all such cases, one should perform the oblation of cooked food.

(5) By this, the rules for offering, giving, and eating are explained; for it is said that "one offers from the cooked, gives from the cooked, and eats from the cooked" in the *pākayajñas*. Therefore, in the *huta*, *prahuta*, and *āhuta* rites, the use of cooked food is required. (6)
He makes the fuel-wood of twenty-one pieces of wood for the sake of providing a form to the sacrifice.
"He sprinkles it with clarified butter; verily, he thereby endows it with splendor," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
The ladle is one cubit long; another [tradition] says it is one forearm long.

Now, it is indeed said: "The ladle (*darvī*) is seized by *Nirṛti*; if one were to offer with a ladle, one would cause the sacrifice to be seized by *Nirṛti*. Therefore, one offers food with a ladle and clarified butter with a *sruva*-spoon; it is known that the ladle has the form of a *vaikaṅkata* tree. Furthermore, they cite this: "Just as a tree born of good soil, with firm roots and well-established, possessing many branches, abundant flowers, and rich in fruit, is put to use by gods, *dānavas*, *gandharvas*, seers (*ṛṣis*), ancestors (*pitṛs*), as well as by birds, bees, mosquitoes, and ants. (10–12)
For thus, all this is established within the *pākayajñas*: the *huta* is to be known as the excellent ground, while the *prahuta* is said to be the root.
(13) The *āhuti* is its foundation for this lofty tree of sacrifice; many are its branches remembered as being well-flowered and laden with fine fruit.

(14) These have been clearly perceived by practitioners who know the true nature of the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas*; indeed, one who is thus conversant with the tree of sacrifice is considered a *śrotriya*. (15)

The wise declare that the act of taking a wife is indeed a ritual (*karman*); he sees a tree endowed with flowers and fruit, possessing many branches, with a good ground, good roots, and a firm foundation. Knowledge is the good ground, conduct is the root, and faith is the foundation.

Forbearance, non-violence, and self-restraint are the branches; truth brings forth the flowers and fruit; and the enjoyment of knowledge is the sacrificial tree of the Buddhas for householders. (16–18)

With an intellect unassailed by desire, having abandoned egoism and greed, he beholds through the two eyes of certainty and resolute application. (19) His singular wrath, resembling a thunderbolt, is called an axe; with that very axe, one should cut away delusion. Therefore, anger must be abandoned in the household. (20) For the home is indeed the root of sacrifices; the home is the cause of freedom from debt; the home is for the sake of honoring the stages of life and for the sake of stability—thus the home is remembered. (21)
"The *pākayajñas*, the *haviryajñas*, and the *somayajñas*—these three are established upon the roots of trees; he who is negligent perishes therein.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the first book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra*.
Now begins the seventh chapter in the first book.

Then, having performed the worship of Arundhatī as part of the wedding ceremony, he undertakes the vow: "O Agni, Lord of Vows, I shall observe the vow of restraint; may I be able to do so, and may it be successful for me. O Vāyu, Lord of Vows! O Āditya, Lord of Vows! O Lord of Vows among vows! I shall observe the vow of restraint; may I be able to do so, and may it be successful for me. (1) Both husband and wife become observers of the vow and sleep on the ground. Between their beds stands a staff of Udumbara wood, smeared with fragrant unguents and encircled by a cloth or a cord, remaining there until the offerings of cooked food are made at night. (2)

When the cooked oblation has been offered, having released the vow, he raises the staff with the mantra: "O Lord of the Forest, you have arisen from the strength of the earth; grow forth with a hundred branches! Speaking of food and vital power through you, may we rejoice in the abundance of wealth and in nourishment.
(3) Then he hands it to the bride with the mantra: "I unite you with offspring, as one mixes *surā* with *māsara*.
(4) The bride receives it with the mantra: "May I be possessed of offspring! (5)

Then he hands him over to the bridegroom with the words: "I unite you with offspring and cattle, as surā is mixed with māṣara. (6) The bridegroom accepts him with the words: "May I be rich in offspring and rich in cattle.
(7) Then, having placed him near the pillar, he approaches by the side. (8)

The lying down [of the student] is well known. On the following day, having taken up the staff and caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made, he releases [the staff] into the waters.

Then, having performed the rites beginning with the smearing of the sacrificial ground for the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), he offers oblations of cooked food with the two verses beginning, "Agni is the head of the world. (Sūtras 9–11)
The rite from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established up to the granting of the boon by the cow.
This is the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha].
Then, after the sun has set, having adorned one another, they lie down upon their beds.
Then he addresses the bride: "This bride is auspicious; come together and behold her. Having bestowed good fortune upon her, depart and go back to your homes.

(15) Then he unites her with a garland of all fragrant scents: "May our minds be united, may our hearts be united, may our navels be united, may our skins be united. I unite you with the bond of desire so that it shall never be released.
(16) Thus ends the seventh chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra.
Now begins the eighth chapter of the first book.
Now, on the tenth day, the Brāhmaṇas are made to hear [the recitation]. 1.

Then, having performed the rites from the smearing of the altar for the sacrifice to the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he offers oblations of cooked food with the two verses beginning, "O All-Gods, O All-Gods. 2.
Then he performs the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
(3) He silently adorns all the shrines with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps. (4) The offering of the bali-oblation is well known. (5)

Having performed the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, sitting on Darbha grass to the west of the fire, holding Darbha grass in his hands, and facing eastward, he should recite the Sāvitrī one thousand times, or one hundred times, or an unlimited number of times, or ten times.
(6) He should study the beginnings of the Vedas, the meters, and the Kūṣmāṇḍa hymns.
(7) Then he offers oblations for the prosperity of the sacrifice with the words: "Svāhā to those who have been sacrificed to; Vaṣaṭ and Svāhā to those who have not been sacrificed to! (8)

Having offered eight *srava* oblations, the procedure from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established up to the granting of the boon by the cow. 9. Now, another [method]: having performed [the rites] up to the placing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he seats two Brahmins for the Viśvedevas, honors them with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, and offers the *caru* of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, dedicating it with the formula: "To the Viśvedevas, svāhā! 10.
Then, having placed the sacred thread over his right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), he asks for a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, iron, bell-metal, or clay. 11.

Having placed it upon *darbha* grass with the tips pointing south, having turned the vessel face upwards and sprinkled it silently with consecrated water, he pours water into it across the strainers while reciting: "O fathers who come by the path of the gods, from the oceans, the waters, and the flowing streams, may you obtain all desires at this sacrifice; may they yield inexhaustible [milk]. For you, the fathers, I take [this]; for you, the grandfathers, I take [this]; for you, the great-grandfathers, I take [this]. (12)

Having shaken out the strainer, he scatters sesame seeds with the mantra: "Thou art sesame, having Soma as thy deity, created by the gods at the Gosava sacrifice; come with the *svadhā* offering like the ancients; gladden these ancestors and these worlds for us; *svadhā*, obeisance! (13).
Then, across the strainer, he pours honey with the three verses beginning "The winds are honey for the one who follows the Law," recited according to their respective meters (14).

Then, having stirred it up with all his fingers, he touches it with the mantra: "Thou art the brilliance of Soma; may my brilliance be like thine; thou art the immortal; protect me from death; protect me from lightning. (15)
If anything should fall upon it, he takes it up with his thumb and his ring finger and casts it away toward this direction, saying: "The biters are driven off; the head of Namuci is cast away.
(16) Then, having touched water, he touches [the vessel] again, saying: "May the divine waters be auspicious for our aid and for our drinking; may they flow toward us for health and well-being. (17)

Then, having honored it with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, and having covered it with *darbha* grass on the southern corners, he scatters sesame seeds and sand upon the places for eating and the seats, saying: "Struck down are the Asuras, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas who dwell upon the earth; let them go elsewhere, wherever their minds are directed. (18) Then he sprinkles it with water, saying: "May the lower, the higher, and the middle ancestors rise up—the Soma-loving Pitṛs who have gone to the life-force (*asu*), the non-malevolent knowers of Truth; may those Pitṛs protect us at our invocations. (19)
Then he invokes the ancestors with the verse: "Come, O Soma-loving ancestors, by your ancient and deep paths, bestowing upon us progeny, wealth, and long life for a hundred autumns. (20)

Then, having summoned the Brahmins and seated them on seats prepared with *darbha* grass, and having performed the well-known rites in the fire, he offers five oblations with the *sruva* ladle: "By means of the waters which flow eastward and those from the north—by these waters, the sustainers of the entire world—I interpose a barrier between myself and my father; *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*! I interpose a barrier by means of the mountains, by the vast earth, by the sky, and by the infinite quarters and protections; I interpose a barrier between myself and my grandfather; *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*!"

I have placed myself between [the worlds] by means of all the seasons, the days and nights with their junctions, the half-months, and the months; I have established a barrier from my great-grandfather—*svadhā*, *namaḥ*, *svāhā*. Whatever of me my mother, acting unfaithfully, has caused to be lost while wandering—that seed may my father take back; let no other come near it—*svadhā*, *namaḥ*, *svāhā*. That limb of yours which the flesh-eater has consumed or which Jātavedas has led away to the worlds, that I cause to enter you again;
be whole with all your limbs, O Fathers—*svadhā*, *namaḥ*, *svāhā*. 21.

Having divided the omentum into three parts, he offers it with a ladle made of *udumbara* wood, saying: "To Soma, accompanied by the Pitṛs, the impetuous one, we offer this oblation. O Vāja, enjoy this our offering; it is well-born for the gods and the Pitṛs. *Svadhā! Namas! Svāhā!* I invoke Yama, who is accompanied by the Aṅgirases, for protection, and who is accompanied by the Pitṛs. O son of Vivasvat, eat this our offering; it is well-born for the gods and the Pitṛs. *Svadhā! Namas! Svāhā!* O Agni Kavyavāhana, you who increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*), worship the Pitṛs. Carry the oblation forward to the gods and to the Pitṛs."
"May there be *svajā* for the oblation to the gods and the ancestors; *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*!

(22) Then, having divided the cake into eight parts and offered three portions according to the ritual procedure for the omentum (*vapā*), he gives the remaining portions to the Brahmins. Having covered these sacrificial portions in the *iḍā*-troughs, he mixes together the rice, meat, and broth with clarified butter. Using a ladle made of *udumbara* wood, he offers them by dipping the ladle into the mixture in the southern half [of the fire], beginning with the mantra: "To the ancestors, *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*," and so on, up to the end of the mantra: "To all [the ancestors], *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*. The mantra is to be modified accordingly. (23)
"To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, svadhā, obeisance, svāhā!

(24) Having served [the food], having followed [the guests] as they have eaten, having circumambulated them from left to right, and having asked permission regarding the remainder, he returns by the same way he came and offers three oblations with the remainder of the food: "That seed which my mother, wandering unfaithful to her vows, caused me to lose—may my father take that seed back; let no other man fall upon it. Svadhā, obeisance, svāhā! (25)

"Whatever my grandmother, acting unfaithfully, caused me to be seduced while she was wandering—may my grandfather take that seed of mine; let no other man come near it. *Svadhā! Homage! Svāhā!* Whatever my great-grandmother, acting unfaithfully, caused me to be seduced while she was wandering—may my great-grandfather take that seed of mine; let no other man come near it. *Svadhā! Homage! Svāhā!*" (26–27)

To the south of the fire, having strewn darbha grass with its tips pointing southward, he offers three balls of food upon them with the remnants of the meal, saying: "This for you, O father, [name], and for those who are your maternal grandfathers, those who are your teachers, those who are your gurus, those who are your friends, those who are your kinsmen, those who are your ministers, and those who are your pupils; and for their wives—for them and for those women—svadhā! Homage! (28)

He offers the second [portion], saying: "This for you, O grandfather, N.N., and for those who are your maternal grandfathers, those who are your teachers, those who are your preceptors, those who are your friends, those who are your kinsmen, those who are your ministers, those who are your pupils, and for their wives—to them, svadhā! Homage! (29) He offers the third [portion], saying: "This for you, O great-grandfather, N.N., and for those who are your maternal grandfathers, those who are your teachers, those who are your preceptors, those who are your friends, those who are your kinsmen, those who are your ministers, those who are your pupils, and for their wives—to them, svadhā! Homage! (30)
On this ground he wipes away the smear: "To those fallen fetuses of ours who wait upon us partaking of blood—to them, self-born, be *svadhā* and obeisance; may they hear us and rejoice!
(31) Those raw, those cooked, and those corrupted ones who fall upon us—to them, self-born, be *svadhā* and obeisance; may they hear us and rejoice!
(32) Those boys, those women, and those unknown ones who fall upon us—to them, self-born, be *svadhā* and obeisance; may they hear us and rejoice! (33)
Then he sprinkles them with the rinsing water while reciting the two verses beginning, "Those who are equal" and "Those who are kinsmen.

(34) Then, with the same rinsing water, he sprinkles three times from right to left over those lumps which are on the sacrificial grass, reciting the verse, "Carrying strength. (35) From this point onward, the procedure is established as the *jaya* offerings and so forth. (36)
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the first book in the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra.
Now begins the ninth chapter of the first book.
Now, indeed, it occurs that for one who is endowed with faith and knows the truth, there may be some excess or deficiency in the sacrifice. 1.

Having prepared the vessel under an auspicious constellation and having invited the Brāhmaṇas, he seats them on seats provided with *darbha* grass and addresses them, saying: "In you alone [shall be performed] the fire-offering (*agnikaraṇa*) and the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). Thus he should speak.

(2) When they have said, "So be it," he gives water with sesame seeds into their hands, which hold the *pavitra* blades. Likewise, having adorned [the food], he gives it; and likewise, when they have finished eating, he gives it. (3) He does not sweep away the remnants of the meal. (4)
Here, he gives three balls of food to Brāhmaṇas from the south.
It is known: "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed all the deities; this Brāhmaṇa is Agni Vaiśvānara.
Thus, for him, it becomes as if an oblation has been offered.

Now, if he should perform [the rite] in the fire—either in the *aupāsana* or the cooking fire—he offers three oblations of food with the formulas: "To Soma, drunk by the fathers, *svadhā*! Adoration! *Svāhā*! "To Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the fathers, *svadhā*! Adoration! *Svāhā*! "To Agni Kavyavāhana, the maker of good offerings, *svadhā*! Adoration! *Svāhā*! (8) Thus, his [offering] becomes as if already sacrificed.
(9) Or else, he may feed Brahmins by means of a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), having caused them to say, "May there be the fulfillment of the resolve. (10)
One should act thus in times of distress, but one should not do so as a regular practice. For those who perform the *śrāddha* rites and the *havis* offerings constantly attend [to these duties].
(11) Regarding this, Bodhāyana says that one should employ a cow.
(12) The ritual procedure for her on the day of fasting (*aupavasathya*) has already been explained. (13)
"This is performed with curd-mixture," says Śālīki;
"with a cake," says Aupamanyava;
"or with an oblation of boiled rice," says Aupamanyavīputra.
"It is known from scripture that one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.

(17) Then, having gone outside and honored the auspicious objects, having worshipped the Brahmins with threefold food and caused them to pronounce blessings, having given the goad and the arrow to the Brahmins, and having circumambulated [the fire] and returned home, he chooses the Adhvaryu priest, saying, "The son of Aṅgiras, Kunakhin.
(18) Thus ends the ninth chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra.
Now, in the first book, the tenth chapter:

Marriage has been explained. Here follows the time for the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*). 1. "From this point forward, one should establish the fires while the father is still living, according to one's faith," says Baudhāyana. 2.
"Whether [the husband] is living or dead, one obtains a wife on the tenth day," says Śālīki. (3) "One does not become a *durbrāhmaṇa*.
(4) Furthermore, they cite this: "He whose Veda and sacrificial altar (*vedi*) are cut off for three generations is indeed called a *durbrāhmaṇa*, as is he who is the husband of a *vṛṣalī*. (5)
Or rather, the *aupāsana* fire should be maintained perpetually; thus one does not become a "bad Brāhmaṇa.
Or, while maintaining the *aupāsana*, having prepared the *brahmaudana* and then discarded it, he brings it back again after performing the consecration (*saṃskāra*) for each respective rite.
But if he is indeed not going to establish the fire, he does not discard it.
Now, it is indeed said: "Aditi, desiring sons, cooked a *brahmaudana* for the Sādhya gods; they gave her the remnants of it, and from eating that she conceived.

(9) For one whose wife in the house has reached her season (*ṛtu*), this is the observance: as at a wedding, for three nights. (10) The difference is only this much: here the wife does not sleep with the staff, nor does she bathe. On the fourth day she bathes and eats of the *brahmaudana*. (11)

For one who desires, "May I become free from debt to the gods, the seers, and the ancestors," this is his vow: it occurs at every seasonal period (*ṛtu*). (12) The *puṃsavana* rite and the constant oblations to Viṣṇu [are performed].
(13) From the *puṃsavana* onwards until delivery, the wife eats food consecrated with clarified butter (*ājya*). (14)

In the eighth month, having bathed with warm water and having offered an oblation to Viṣṇu, he undertakes the vow. 15. It is known from tradition that she then becomes one who gives birth to a son. 16.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra.
Now, the eleventh chapter in the first book:
If he becomes a father of a son, having performed the well-known birth-rite (*jātakarman*) in the *aupāsana* fire, he offers the *phalīkaraṇa* oblation elsewhere; that becomes the *sūtaka* fire.
He maintains it for ten days.

Then, on the dawning of the ninth day, having melted clarified butter in the *sūtakāgni* fire and purified it, he raises the pair [of poles] with the verse: "The knowledge born of Brahman... (RV 10.72.1).
(3) Then he raises the water-pot with the formula: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ om.

(4) Then he consigns it into the waters with the verse: "I send you forth to the ocean; go to your own source, O imperishable ones! May I be without flaw in my offspring; may my seed not be spilled. (5)

Then, having returned by the same way he came, he stands before the *sūtakāgni* fire with the mantra: "O youngest one, be mindful of this word of ours, which is most bountiful and offered with self-sustaining power (*svadhā*). One person reviles, another praises; I, your worshipper, revere your body, O Agni.
(6) Then he stands before the woman who has given birth to a son with the mantra: "May the wise patron, the giver of wealth, the lord of riches, be awakened. Drive away from us all enmities. (7)
Then he makes the boy stand up with the verse: "Arise, O Brahmaṇaspati! We, seeking the gods, call upon you. May the bounteous Maruts come forward; O Indra, be swift in our company.
(8) Then, taking him and going out, he causes him to gaze at the sun with four verses: "Up from the darkness," "Up that [sun]," "The bright," and "That highest step of Viṣṇu.

(9) Then, returning by the same way he came, having placed the boy in the hand of his mother, he offers oblations of clarified butter into the *sūtaka* fire, verse by verse, from the beginning of the invitatory verse: "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning. (10)
"You cast away the fire of birth.
(VS 3.22) "O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation," with these words he either consigns [the fire] into the two kindling woods or churns it at the initiation ceremony.
Then he worships the domestic fire (*aupāsana*) with two verses: "O Agni, you purify lives... and "O Agni, purify yourself, O skillful one... (14).
With the verse containing the word *jyotiṣmatī* (full of light), he utters the name of his son; "He thus makes him an eater of food," so says the Brāhmaṇa (15).
Then, having smelled him on the head, he consecrates him with five sections beginning with "Agni is long-lived" (16).
Or, having returned from a journey, he consecrates his son with these very same [mantras].
(17) The rising [from confinement] on the tenth day is well known. (18) The naming ceremony takes place on the tenth or the twelfth day. (19)
According to some, the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), the going out (*upaniṣkrāmaṇa*), and the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) are completed simply by the feeding of Brāhmaṇas;
according to others, they are completed simply by the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*).
The tonsure (*caula*) and the initiation (*upanayana*) are well known [from other sources].
Thus ends the eleventh chapter of the first book in the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra.
Now begins the twelfth chapter of the first book:
Now follow the prohibitions for one who has been initiated. 1.
One should not eat the remnants of another, except in the case of one's father or elder brother.

(2) One should not eat together with a woman. (3) Regarding honey, meat, food from a *śrāddha* ceremony, food from a house of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), food where ten days have not yet passed [since a death], the milk of a *sandhinī* cow, mushrooms, exudations from trees, salt prepared from saline earth (*vilayana*), food belonging to a group (*gaṇānna*), and food belonging to a courtesan (*gaṇikānna*)—in these cases, there must be a re-initiation (*punassaṃskāra*). (4)
"Going to forbidden places," so say some.

(5) Furthermore, they cite this: "A Brāhmaṇa who has gone to Saurāṣṭra, Sindhu-Sauvīra, Avanti, or the Deccan deserves a rite of re-initiation. (6) Now, we shall explain the rites of re-initiation. (7)

Then, having performed the rites from the drawing of the lines for the deity’s altar up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he takes a fuel-stick of *palāśa* wood, anoints it with clarified butter, and while making him place it on the fire, he causes him to recite: "May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus kindle you again; may the Brahmins, O leader of wealth, [kindle you] with sacrifices. Increase our bodies with clarified butter; may the desires of the sacrificer come true—Svāhā!
(8) Then he offers two oblations as an expiation for the violation of the vow (*avratya*), with the two verses: "Whatever deficiency has occurred in my self, Agni has given back my sight" (9).
Then he offers an oblation from the cooked food with the verse: "Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues" (10).
Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with the three verses beginning "With that purifier by which the gods," each according to its meter (11).
The rite from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established as complete up to the giving of the cow as a boon (12).

Now, another [procedure]: having performed [the rites] up to the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), and having placed a fuel-stick of *palāśa* wood upon the fire, he offers an oblation for the expiation of the violation of the vow (13).

Then he offers oblations with the Vyāhṛtis. 14. Now another [method]: by the mere word of a Brāhmaṇa, having consecrated clarified butter a hundred times with the Sāvitrī and consumed it, one becomes purified through the performance of the penance. 15.
Or one may eat the leavings of the teacher. 16.

Moreover, they cite this: "Shaving, the giving of sacrificial fees, the girdle, the staff, the deerskin, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—these cease when the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) is performed.
These rites of re-consecration have now been explained.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the first book of the *Bodhāyana Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra*.
Now, the thirteenth chapter of the first book:

Having studied the Veda, one who is about to bathe prepares the following items: a grass mat and a pillow, a barber, a razor, pieces of wood for a seat, a covering cloth, small wooden sticks, a tooth-cleansing twig, warm water and cold water, the powder of all fragrant substances, collyrium, a garland, a mirror, an unwashed garment, an outer cloak, an inner garment, a jujube-stone amulet with a gold setting, a water-pot, two earrings, a staff, sandals, an umbrella, and the hide of a bull entirely red; these are his requirements.
The ritual requisites are prepared. 1. Now follows the deliberation regarding the bath. 2.

"One should bathe under Rohiṇī"—this is one view; for this lunar mansion belongs to Prajāpati, so he has bathed under the very lunar mansion belonging to Prajāpati, and furthermore, he ascends all heights. 3.

"One should bathe under Tiṣya"—this constellation belongs to Bṛhaspati; thus he has bathed under Bṛhaspati's own constellation, thinking, "May I be impelled by Bṛhaspati. 4. "One should bathe under the two Uttaraphalgunīs"—this constellation belongs to Bhaga; thus he has bathed under Bhaga's own constellation, thinking, "May I be fortunate. 5. "One should bathe under Hasta"—this constellation belongs to Savitṛ; thus he has bathed under Savitṛ's own constellation, thinking, "May I be impelled by Savitṛ. 6.

"One should bathe under Citrā"—this is one view; for this lunar mansion belongs to Indra, so he bathes under a lunar mansion belonging to Indra; furthermore, [he thinks], "May I be variegated (citra) with offspring and cattle. "One should bathe under Viśākhā"—this is another view; for this lunar mansion belongs to Indra and Agni, so he bathes under a lunar mansion belonging to Indra and Agni; furthermore, [he thinks], "May I be forked (viśākha) with offspring and cattle."

During one of these waxing fortnights, having entered the cow-pen before the rising of the sun, the sun shall not shine upon him that day; for he is the face of those who have bathed, and he shines with brilliance and glory.
(9) They enclose the pen with a skin, hairy side inward.

(10) Having kindled the fire in the middle of the eastern half of the pen and strewn grass around it, they bring all these ritual materials at once; for according to this Brāhmaṇa passage, "all [materials] together, because all human [actions are performed together]. (11)
The Brahmin sits down to the south.
(12) To the north, he places a water-pot and a fuel-stick of *palāśa* wood.
(13) Having spread out an *erakā* grass mat with its fringes directed toward the north behind the fire, he sits upon it facing east. (14)
To the north, the barber [should stand]. 15.
To the north, the pillow. 16.
One should give alms until midday. 17.

"Even if there were a barren cow here, one should cook it; having anointed a fuel-stick of *pālāśa* wood with clarified butter, he places it on the fire at midday with the verse: 'This hymn I fashion for the worthy Jātavedas with my inspired thought, as one fashions a chariot; for his providence toward us is auspicious in the assembly; may we not come to harm in your friendship, O Agni, Svāhā!

(19) Then, on an *airakā* plant, he lies down facing north with the formula: 'The triple life-span of Jamadagni, the triple life-span of Kaśyapa, the triple life-span of Agastya, the triple life-span of the Ṛṣis, that which is the triple life-span of the gods—may that triple life-span be mine! (20)"
He recites over the moistening [of the hair]: "May your touch be auspicious to me. (21) He consecrates the razor:
"Razor is your name; the axe is your father; homage be to you; do not harm me. (22) He recites over the shaving:
"In that you shave with the razor, O shaver, you shave the hair and beard; make my face radiant; do not steal away my life-span. (23)
First he shaves his beard, then the armpits, then the hair of the body, and finally the hair on the other parts of the limbs.

For it is from these [parts] that people first depart in old age during their lifetime; thus they become eaters of food throughout their life who, knowing this, have their body hair shaved. If he is about to have his body hair shaved, he should, after having his head hair and beard shaved, gather the body hair and clip his nails.

Then, having gathered these together, he hands them to the student (brahmacārin) and says: "Having taken these, deposit them on a clump of *darbha* grass or at the root of an *udumbara* tree. He deposits them there. 26. Sitting to the west of the fire facing east, he loosens his girdle (*mekhalā*) with the mantra: "I loosen this bond of Varuṇa. 27.
To one who is his son or a resident pupil (*antevāsin*) present there, he hands it over and says: "Having taken this, deposit it on a *nyagrodha* tree or at the root of an *udumbara* tree. 28.
There he places those two [stones] with the formula: "Here I conceal the sin of N.N., the son of N.N., by means of this pain, away from his enemies for the sake of the one who follows.

(29) Having run forward with the *vṛkala* plants, he causes the tamed [animals] to run about for the sake of food, [saying]: "O Bhaga, drive away those who have come together; let him enter my mouth for the sake of luster and for the sake of fortune. (30) He pours both kinds of water together: hot water into which cold water is poured, for the sake of distinguishing between the divine and the human. (31)

Having offered them with joined palms, he sprinkles [the student] with water using the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*, the three verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*, and from this Brāhmaṇa passage: "Man is indeed constituted in six ways.

(32) Then, having mixed together all fragrant substances ground into powder, he sprinkles [him] three times with the formula: "Homage to Śāka and Jañjabha; to those deities who are the seizers. (33) He should anoint [himself] with the formula: "The fragrance which is among the Apsarases, and the glory which is among the Gandharvas—the divine and human fragrance, may that enter me here. (34)
He puts on an unwashed garment with the formula: "O my own body, enter me! O auspicious body, enter me! In this very same way in the evening, and in this very same way from then onwards.

Then, having strung this jujube berry (*bādara*) together with gold upon a thread as a support, and having placed it in a ladle, he winds the thread around the handle of the ladle and offers it with the formula: "This herb, *oṣadhi*, protecting, conquering, powerful—may she make me possessed of the luster of Soma, the luster of the Sun, and the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); may she make me one who possesses the luster of sacred knowledge and an eater of food, Svāhā! || 36 ||
Then he causes him to be sprinkled with water from a vessel, saying: "May we, through you, cross over all enemies, as one crosses over streams of water.
(37) Having said, "You are the releaser," he carries [the vessel] across diagonally; for, according to this Brāhmaṇa, "they bind the victim facing backward for the sake of separation.

(38) Then, having threaded these two earrings onto a string, placed them on the ladle, and wound the string around the handle of the ladle, he offers an oblation, saying: "Granting long life, granting splendor, bestowing increase of wealth, and breaking forth—may this gold enter this man for the sake of splendor and victory; may it bestow this wealth, Svāhā! (39)

He offers the second oblation with: "Like a female dog, I have taken the name of my father's gold. May it make me resplendent with the luster of Soma, resplendent with the luster of the Sun; may it make me possessed of the luster of sacred knowledge and an eater of food, Svāhā! (40) He offers the third oblation with: "O high-flying steed, conqueror of armies, victor in the assembly, winner of wealth—whatever prosperities and riches are contained within gold, Svāhā!

(41) He offers the fourth oblation with: "The sovereign power and the self-ruling power, the blessings that are in our house, and the fortune that is at the head of the kingdom—with that we unite you, Svāhā! (42)

He offers the fifth oblation with: "Bestow glory upon me among the Brāhmaṇas; bestow glory upon me among the Kṣatriyas; bestow glory upon me among the Vaiśyas and Śūdras. I am this glory of yours, svāhā!
(43) Then he causes these two [the hair-tuft and the amulet] to float in a vessel of water with the verse: "May we, through thee, overcome all...
(44) Taking the space between those two, he ties them to the right ear with these five verses beginning: "Conducive to long life, conducive to luster... (45)
Then he turns it around him with the words: "With the seasons, with the seasonal periods, with the nourishment of the year—with these I follow after you.
(46) In the same way, he should tie on the ear-ornament (*pravarta*) in the left ear.

(47) Then he puts on the garland (*sraj*) with the words: "O beautiful one, ascend my head, adorning my face; adorn my face and grant me abundant fortune. You whom Jamadagni took away for faith, for love, and for another—this very you I put on for splendor and for fortune. (48)

"When he applies collyrium made from *traikakuda*—since *traikakuda* collyrium is produced upon the Himavat—he says: 'With that I anoint you both; may there be mountain-like luster in me. (49) "When he looks into a mirror, he says: 'My mind which has gone far away, as I look into the mirror—this very thing I see within me; may it be life-giving and full of luster for me. (50) "Then he puts on his two sandals: with 'Thou art heaven' on the right foot, and with 'Thou art earth' on the left. (51)

Then he takes up the staff with the words: "O friend, protect me. (52) He takes up the umbrella with the words: "Thou art divine, thou art the fair-winged bird; protect me from the intermediate space.

(53) Then, having gone outside, he worships the quarters with the verse: "O goddesses, you who are six and wide, make us spacious; O All-gods, act like heroes. May we not be abandoned by our offspring nor by our bodies; may we not fall into the power of the enemy, O King Soma! (54)
"Attentive to the moon," [he says].
Wherever he desires, there he goes; this is the *samāvartana* (the rite of returning home).
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the first book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra*.
Now, the fourteenth chapter in the first book.
Now follows the silent return home (*samāvartana*) for one who has performed the vow-bath (*vratasnātaka*) but has not studied the Veda.

Having bathed at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), having kindled the fire and strewn grass around it, he offers a fuel-stick of *palāśa* wood, anointed with clarified butter, at midday with the verse beginning, "This hymn of praise... (*imaṃ stomaṃ*).

Having performed the shaving in silence and the gathering of the ritual materials in silence, he touches the right wheel of the chariot with the formula, "Thou art the *rathantara*"; the left [wheel] with, "Thou art the *bṛhat*";
[3] he touches the middle [part] of the chariot with, "Thou art the *vāmadevya*";
[4] he addresses the chariot as it starts moving with, "O Aśvins, the chariot is for our welfare; may the chariot not harm me in sorrow nor in joy. [5]
In the absence of a chariot, having touched water, he touches the ground, saying: "Here is stability, here is support, here is delight, here is enjoyment.
(6) Then, having touched water, he touches his heart, saying: "In me [reside] the senses and vigor.
(7) Having mixed water with rice or barley grains, he gives it to the student. (8)
He accepts it with the words: "May he come to me with splendor and glory.

(9) A Brāhmaṇa [should accept it] with the words: "May he come to me with splendor and glory; unite me with what is dear, as the lord of cattle and of progeny. Having touched that [water], he should speak.
(10) He pours that water, previously poured out, to the east. (11)
Then he should present the *arghya*—either mixed with curds, honey, clarified butter, and water, or mixed with curds, honey, clarified butter, water, and milk—with the formula: "This is the *arghya*.
(12) The student consecrates the *arghya* with the mantra: "May he protect me; may they protect me; may he enjoy me.
(13) Then he receives it with both hands with the mantra: "May he come to me with splendor. (14)
If anything should fall into it, he gathers it with his thumb and his ring finger and casts it away in this direction, saying: "May it not reach the sacrificer.

(15) Then, having touched water and having stirred [the remainder] with all his fingers, he eats it: first, saying, "I take this strength from you"; second, "Make me the best, the overlord"; third, "You are Soma; make me a drinker of Soma"; fourth, "You are food; make me one who has food. (16) Having eaten thus four times, he should sip water three times; he should not consume it all, nor should he reach satiety. (17)
"One should give the remainder to him whom one desires for one's own welfare.

(18) Then he consecrates with a mantra the cow tied by a rope to the ear: "Slay my sin, O cow, who has come near. (19) Then he should release the cow with the words: "The cow is to be a milch-cow. (20)
Then he eats that which has been brought to him, saying: "O Brahman, I eat thee.
(21) Then he eats the flour mixed with water that has been brought, saying: "O Brahman, I eat thee.

(22) In this very same manner, for those who are incapable—such as the dull-witted, the deaf, the mute, the blind, the hunchbacked, and so forth—he should silently place a fuel-stick on the fire and perform the remainder of the rite silently. (23)
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter in the first book:
There are three types of *snātakas*: the *vedasnātaka*, the *vratasnātaka*, and the *vedavratasnātaka*. 1.

Now, from this point forward, these [articles] become his permanent possessions: the sacred fire (aupāsana), a staff, a water-pot, sandals, an umbrella, two garments, two sacrificial threads, a turban, a deerskin, and an inner garment.
(2) He should go out from and enter the village by the eastern road, remaining silent; or he may do so by the northern road. (3) He should release his speech only outside [the village]. (4)

He should study either a *praśna* or an *anuvāka*. (5) Devoted to the Veda and constant in his Vedic duties, he should eat after having performed the libations (*tarpaṇa*) for the gods, the seers, and the ancestors.

(6) By day he should not wear a turban, but by night he may wear one; and during the voiding of urine and feces, he should wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*nivītin*), while at other times it should always be worn over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*). (7)
8. One should sip water while standing or while stooping.
9. During the two twilights, one should remain outside the village, seated and restrained in speech.
10. Until sexual union with a wife, they are *snātakas*; from that point onward, they are householders.
One should engage in worldly affairs through the Vedic vows—namely, the Kaumāra, the Māheśvara, and the Dhānvantara—in order to ensure the non-interruption [of the lineage].
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter in the first book.

If he does not maintain the *aupāsana* fire, then, having offered oblations of clarified butter with the *vyāhṛtis* until the tenth day, one who is about to establish the sacred fires prepares a *brahmaudana* and discards that [fire]. Having consecrated it again for each respective rite, he brings it back. However, if he is not about to establish the fires, he does not discard it.

In that fire into which one leads [the student], in that [fire] the observance of vows is performed, in that the return ceremony (*samāvartana*) is performed, in that the taking of the hand in marriage is performed, and in that the domestic rites (*gṛhya-karmāṇi*) are carried out. Some say that the sacraments of offspring (*prajā-saṃskārāḥ*) are also performed in that [fire].
(4) This very [fire], from the initiation (*upanayana*) onwards, is offered oblations of fuel-sticks with the *vyāhṛtis* until the return ceremony.
(5) From the return ceremony onwards, it is offered oblations of clarified butter with the *vyāhṛtis* alone until the taking of the hand in marriage. (6)
From the time of taking the hand [in marriage] onwards, with rice or barley.
(7) He offers these two oblations with his hand, saying: "To Agni, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! in the evening.
(8) Also in the morning, saying: "To Sūrya, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! (9)
He offers [the oblation] with one of the various materials used for the Agnihotra.

10. Now follows his well-known Pārvaṇa Āgneya sthālīpāka; its implements are: a mortar and pestle, a black antelope skin, a winnowing basket, a wooden sword (sphya), a cooking pot, a butter-pot, a large and small ladle, a spoon, and a stirring-stick.
11. Then, on the new moon day, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is performed according to the established rule. 12.
The term *gārhapatya* does not exist here [in this context].
(13) By this, his status as a performer of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices is established. (14) The fire beginning with the initiation (*upanayana*) is called the *aupāsana*. (15)
Some say it begins with the taking of the hand [in marriage].
16. When [the fire] has gone out, it should be maintained by kindling, or churned, or brought from the house of one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*).
17. And when it has gone out, there is fasting for either the wife or the husband. 18.
Or rather, one should offer a single oblation with the verse, "And of her, O Agni... (RV 3.29.2).
Next is the expiation for an oblation not offered: "May the mind, as light, enjoy [the offering]... (RV 1.18.6). Next is the expiation for an omission: "O Agni, lead us to the gods... (RV 1.189.1).
Then follows his expiation for a violation of the vow (*avratyaprāyaścitta*): "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows; whatever we have done against you... (VS 10.28).
Then follows his expiation for an unknown offense (*anājñātaprāyaścitta*): "The unknown [sin], measured by a man... (VS 10.29).
Now, if the fire-pan (*ukhā*) should break, he addresses it with the mantra: "Unbroken is the Gharma, the giver of life; from where it was taken, there it has gone again" (VS 10.30).

Then, having melted the clarified butter and purified it, and having taken four portions into the *sruva* ladle, he offers the *santanī* oblation with the verse: "The fuel, the altar, and all the enclosing sticks follow the life-span of the sacrifice. Those thirty-three threads which have been stretched out and which rejoice in this sacrifice with their own inherent power—to them I restore what was severed; *svāhā*! (25) Then he brings another [ladle] with the formula: "May the *gharma* reach the gods! (26) He uses the *manasvatī* [verse] for one day, the *vāruṇī* for two days, the *tantumatī* for three days, and the *abhyāvartinī* verses for four days, up to twelve days. (27)
If [the sacred fire] has been interrupted for twelve days, it must be re-established (punarādheya). 28.

Now, if it should be re-established after being interrupted for twelve days, the materials are brought from the original source; the Brahman priest brings them with the syllable *praṇava* and gives the impulse with the *praṇava*. 29.

Having brought the materials for the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) as they are available to a site that has been smeared and strewn with sand, and having piled them up with the *vyāhṛtis*, he adds fuel and worships with the verse, "O Agni, thou art beloved by these... (*juṣṭo damūnāḥ*). 30.

Then, having swept around the fire from left to right, sprinkled water around it, and spread the sacrificial grass, he melts the clarified butter, purifies it, heats the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and wipes them together. Having taken four portions of clarified butter into the *sruk*, he offers the *pūrṇāhuti* (full-offering) into the fire that has been encircled by a line of ashes—or even if not so encircled—with the verse, "Seven are thy [tongues], O Agni" (RV 10.87.1).
At the *pūrṇāhuti*, he gives a boon: a cow, a bull, a draft-ox, a bronze vessel, gold, or a garment.
Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers three *tantumatī* verses separately: "Stretching the thread, awaken, O Agni; there are thirty-three threads.
(33) Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers four *abhyāvartinī* verses separately: "O Agni, you who turn back; O Agni Aṅgiras, return with vigor and with wealth.
(34) Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers the *manasvatī* verse: "Mind is the light... (35)
Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers it with the *prājāpatyā* verse: "O Prajāpati, none other than you... (RV 10.121.10).
||36|| Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers it with the *anukhyā* verse: "Agni has looked along the forefront of the dawns... (RV 7.8.1).
||37|| Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) with the verse: "And [the oblation] which, O Agni... (VS 10.24). ||38||
Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers the *jyotiṣmatī* oblation with the verse, "Up from the darkness... (RV 1.50.10).
Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers the *āyurdā* oblation with the verse, "O Agni, giver of life... (VS 3.16).
Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers two *mindā* oblations with the verses, "Whatever deficiency has occurred in my self... (VS 5.2) and "Agni has given back my sight... (VS 5.3).

Furthermore, having taken four portions, he offers the *vyāhṛtis* both individually and collectively. (42) Or, with a single oblation, he performs the reconnection with the verse, "May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus... (43).
Then follows its mounting upon the road with the verse, "This is your womb, appropriate for the season... (44).
Or, having placed [the fire] upon two kindling sticks (*araṇī*) and churned it out, he should offer the oblation.

(45) Alternatively, there is the placing [of the fire] within oneself: having placed it within oneself with the verse, "O Agni, that body of yours which is worthy of sacrifice," and having descended [the fire] into the common fire with the verse, "Descend, O Jātavedas," he should offer the oblation.

(46) Or again, having placed [the fire] upon a fuel-stick (*samidh*) with the verse, "This is your seasonal womb," and having added fuel to the common fire with the two verses, "Being invoked" and "Awake, O Agni," he should offer the oblation. (47)

When the fires have been consigned within himself, he should not eat, he should not drink, he should not sleep on a raised bed, he should not immerse himself in water, and he should not engage in sexual intercourse.

(48) He may eat at will, he may drink at will, and he may indeed sleep on a raised bed; [he should avoid wood] from the *pālāśa*, the *aśvattha*, the *khadira*, or the *udumbara* trees. (49) For these [fires], the consigning [into oneself] is accomplished by this very method. (50)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra.

If he maintains the *aupāsana* fire, there are three types of *snātaka*s: namely, the *vratasnātaka*, who has studied the Veda and is about to perform the ceremonial bath; the *upanīta*, who has been initiated; and the one who, having given birth to a son, [performs the rites]. Herein is the time for the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*). Now, indeed, it is said: "something. Then, on the tenth day, [is the time] for marriage. In all *darvihoma* offerings, [one should act] in a pure and level place. Then, on the following day, [is the time] for the gods. And Viṣṇu, indeed, [is mentioned]. Now, indeed, it is said: "by means of everything, indeed. Now, indeed, it is said: "being born. 16.

Now, indeed, it is said: "being born"; now, indeed, it is said: "by everything, indeed"; Viṣṇu and indeed; then on the following day of the gods; then in a pure and level place; in all *darvī*-oblations; then regarding the marriage; then on the tenth day; now, indeed, it is said: "something"; here is the time for the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*); if she has given birth to a son; then regarding one who has been initiated (*upanīta*); having studied the Veda and being about to perform the ceremonial bath (*snāsyan*); then regarding one who has completed his vows (*vratasnātaka*); there are three kinds of those who have taken the bath (*snātaka*); if he does not maintain the domestic fire (*aupāsana*). 16.
Thus ends the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra.
Now begins the first chapter of the second book.

Now, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* (pot-offering) of fresh rice and barley that has not yet been offered, having kindled the fire and strewn grass around it, and having performed the two *āghāra* libations and the two *ājyabhāga* portions, one should offer oblations to the deities of the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice—namely Indra and Agni, the Viśve Devas, Heaven and Earth, and Soma—with Sviṣṭakṛt as the fourth. 1.
One may, at will, offer the *ājyāni* oblations before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
(2) The two mantras for consuming [the remnants] are well-known. (3) Having performed the *vaiśvadeva* rite and having given [portions] to the Brahmins, there is the consumption. (4)
By this, the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice for all plants is explained, with the exception of *śyāmāka* and bamboo-grain (*veṇuyava*).
(5) There is a *caru* of *śyāmāka* for Soma, or one of bamboo-grain for Agni-Indra, or one for the Viśvedevas.
(6) The mantras for the partaking of the food are the same. (7)
Then, having given fruits, roots, and edible items to the Brahmins, he himself consumes them.

(8) Flowers and other new things, having been given to the Brahmins, are then used [by him]. (9) Now, every six months, or at the commencement of a solstice, having performed the rites from the tracing of the altar for the sacrifice to the gods up to the pouring of water for the *praṇītā* vessels, and having heated and wiped the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and having taken four portions of clarified butter into the *sruk*, he offers the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* oblation while holding the vessel; then, having cooked the *āmikṣā* curd-mixture, he requests either boiled rice or milk-rice that has been cooked. (10)
Having sprinkled it [with water], he places it on the fire. 11.
He pours out the clarified butter (ājya). 12.
Then he places the clarified butter on the fire. 13.
Having carried fire around both [the pot and the implements], he cleanses the stirring-spoon and the dipping-spoon. 14.

Then, having cooked this sacrificial porridge (caru), having sprinkled it with clarified butter, and having removed it from the fire towards the north, he pours butter over it once it has been set down. 15.

Having performed the rites from the laying of the enclosing sticks up to the "mouth of the fire" (the oblation to Agni), he offers a spoonful with the Svāhā-call before the [usual] Svāhā-invocations, saying: "Svāhā to the gods! 16.

Then, having taken four portions into the *sruk* ladle, he offers the omentum with the mantra: "O Jātavedas, go to the gods with the omentum; for you have become the first Hotṛ-priest. Increase our bodies with clarified butter; may the gods eat the oblation consecrated by Svāhā—Svāhā!

(17) Then he offers a spoonful of oblation above the Svāhā-consecration with the formula: "To the gods, Svāhā! (18) Then he offers from the cooked portion with the formulas: "To Indra and Agni, Svāhā! To Agni, Svāhā! (19)

Then he offers the *vājina* with: "O drinkers of ghee, drink the ghee; O drinkers of fat, drink the fat! You are the oblation of the intermediate space; *svāhā* to you for the intermediate space, *svāhā*! (20) Then he offers of the *āmikṣā* with: "Indra and Agni, the luminous realms of heaven; you struck down Vṛtra. (21) Then he offers the *vājina* to the quarters with: "The quarters, the fore-quarters, the by-quarters, the intermediate quarters, the upper quarters—*svāhā*! Homage to the quarters, *svāhā* to the quarters! (22)
Then he offers a spoonful from the speckled butter with the formula, "To Vanaspati, svāhā!
(23). Then, from the *āmikṣā* itself, he performs the *sauviṣṭakṛta* offering with the two *sviṣṭavat* formulas.
(24). Then, having taken four portions into the ladle, he offers eleven oblations in separate draws with the formula, "Go to the ocean, svāhā! (25).
From the *jaya* oblation onwards, [the rite] is established up to the granting of the boon of the *mādhenu* cow.
(26) By this, his status as one who has performed the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) is attained.

(27) By means of the *pārvaṇa* [rite], other rites with a single deity are explained; by means of the *āgrayaṇa*, those with many deities; and by means of the *āmikṣā*, the animal sacrifice is explained; those rites which are not included are understood from traditional practice (*ācāra*). (28)

The deities are as prescribed [in the ritual manuals]. (29) The subsidiary offerings (upahoma) are made between the oblation to Agni and that to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. (30) In the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, the Viśvedevas are the deities; on the full moon day, the Paurṇamāsī offering belongs to whichever full moon day the rite is performed. (31)
At the commencement and at the conclusion [of the sacrifice], the seer who is known [is the primary one].
(32) Sadasaspati is the second.
(33) They prescribe the oblation for [food] that is not mixed with alkaline salt, pungent salt, or inferior food, even when prepared by a woman. (34)
The optional offerings and the *bali* oblations are performed according to the instruction.
Furthermore, regarding the optional rites, it is said in the Brāhmaṇa: "Prajāpati created offspring; once they were created, Indra and Agni hid them away"—from this [passage].
Those which are *puroḍāśas* there are *carus* here; the *yājyās* and *puronuvākyās* are according to the respective deities; that which is the *vaṣaṭkāra* there is the *svāhākāra* here.

The establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the fire-oblation (*agnihotra*), the new- and full-moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the first-fruits offering (*āgrayaṇa*), the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), and the Soma sacrifice—this is the ladle-offering (*darvīhoma*) accompanied by the *āghāra* libations.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the rules pertaining to the *agnihotra*.
It is established that one should perform all of this with the offering of the *svāhā* exclamation.
Having performed [the rites] up to the putting on of the garment, he offers to the deity with the formula, "To such-and-such, svāhā! (41).
Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the second [deity]. (42).
He offers twice, wipes [the vessel] twice, eats twice, moves away, sips water, and licks [the vessel]. (43).

This is the Āgnihotrika. 44. Now, therefore, we shall explain the *apūrva* (the unprecedented). 45. One should offer the *daśahotṛ* formula in the evening and morning; the *caturhotṛ* at the *parvan* sacrifices; the *ajyānīs* at the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifices; the *pañcahotṛ* at the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices; the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* at the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*); the *saptahotṛ* at the beginning of the seasons (*ṛtumukha*) and at the *ṛtumukhīya* Soma sacrifice. 46. One should offer the *daśahotṛ* with milk; the *caturhotṛ* with food; the *ajyānīs* with milk-rice (*pāyasa*); the *pañcahotṛ* with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*); the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* with curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*); the *ṛtumukhīya* with speckled butter; and the *saptahotṛ* with Soma.

This is the unprecedented *homa* for those who are devoted to the *aupāsana* fire, who see things as they truly are, who have no further desires, and who are full of faith; it is intended either for the consecration of offspring or for those with limited knowledge. With ordinary oblations, he offers whatever he desires; that becomes an offering made for him. 47. Thus the unprecedented [rite] has been explained. 48. Thus ends the first chapter of the second book in the *Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra* of Bodhāyana.
Now begins the second chapter of the second book.
Now it is indeed said: "The *nivīta* is for men, the *prācīnāvīta* for the ancestors, and the *upavīta* for the gods.
How, then, should one understand these?

Having grasped the neck and the heart from above with both shoulders, he holds [the thread] below the heart and above the navel with his two thumbs; that is the *nivīta* for humans—by this it is meant that it belongs to the *ṛṣis*.
(3) By this, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana and others are explained. (4) Among them, the seven *ṛṣis* become kings; those who constitute their lineage here are "humans. (5)

Now, the duties for which the *nivīta* [mode] is prescribed are: the libation to the seers (*ṛṣis*), sexual intercourse, the sacraments of offspring, the voiding of urine and feces—except during the *homa*—the carrying out of the dead, and whatever other human activities there may be; in these, the *nivīta* is that which is suspended around the neck.

(6) Having taken hold of the right side above the waist, including the neck, the heart, and the back, and placing it below the left hand, it is the *prācīnāvīta*, belonging to the ancestors (*pitṛs*). This is said to be for those who have died.
(7) By this, Vaiśampāyana and others are also explained. (8)
Among them, Soma Pitṛmān, Yama Aṅgirasvat, and Agni Kavyavāhana are the kings; those who exist after death are the ancestors (pitaraḥ). 9.
Placing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, grasping the neck, heart, and back, and keeping it below the right hand—this is for the gods; by this, it is said to be for the immortals themselves.
10. By this, the Brahmayajña and others are explained. 11.
Among them, Indra, Soma, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera become kings; that which is their continuity in the hereafter is the gods. 12.

How indeed should one understand the *yajñopavīta* (sacrificial thread)? 13. This [thread] is placed below the right hand; for this right hand is the sacrifice (*yajña*). Regarding the word *yajña*: because it is used in the senses of worshiping the gods, forming a connection, and giving, and because they perform these [acts], therefore it is called *yajña*. 14.
Speech is the sacrifice; Agni is its presiding deity (adhidaivata), and since he is present here [in the thumb], therefore it is the sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta).
And this thumb is Viṣṇu, who is the presiding deity of the sacrifice; therefore it becomes so, both because of that and because it is a sacred site (tīrtha).
Speech itself is the sacrifice, for whatever one speaks with speech, one accomplishes that by means of this [sacrificial thread].
The sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) has been explained. 18.
Thus ends the second chapter of the second book in the *Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra* of Baudhāyana.
Now begins the third chapter of the second book.

Now, it is indeed said: "The Brāhmaṇa is the Ekahotṛ; he is the sacrifice. This very Kusindhya is the one authorized [for this]; the Daśahotṛ is his foundation. Whatever exists is his inner self; the Kusindhya is the self, the sacrifice is the supreme self, and he is the Puruṣa. "All this that has been, that which is to be, and that which will be—this is the Agnihotra; that indeed is the Kusindhya who is authorized; that is his Daśahotṛ as the foundation; he is the sacrifice; he abides in the self;
