his upper garment is the *yajñopavīta* (sacrificial thread). 1.

Now, indeed, it is said: "The knower of sacrifice becomes the knower of all; the sacrifice is everything," so says the Śruti. Therefore, those who perceive reality delight in reflections upon the sacrificial rites. Regarding this, *agnihotra*, *kusindha*, *ekahotṛtva*, *sthūri*, and *kevala* are words denoting the same meaning; they are characterized by faith (*śraddhā*). It is known from scripture that "faith is water" and "water is established in [the waters]. These—namely the sacrifice, the attainment of the *agnihotra*, the attainment of the *kusindha*, the state of the single hotṛ, the state of the *sthūri*, and the state of being absolute (*kaivalya*)—are that Brahman, the single syllable, the supreme Brahman, which is "Om," which is Brahman. 2.

Now, it is indeed said: "The *brahman* is anointed; by its anointing, one drives away evil through ritual action (*karman*). Because of this driving away of attachments, the praise of the *brāhmaṇa* is proclaimed. Thus, there is both the state of being a *brāhmaṇa* and the state of being the sole Hotṛ priest. Because the tongue has the nature of water (*āpyatva*), it is, in its internal (*adhyātma*) aspect, the locus that expresses taste; in its external (*adhibhūta*) aspect, it is the same because of the unity of intellect and action; and in its divine (*adhidaivata*) aspect, it is the same because of the unity of Agni and Soma. Since this Soma is indeed the Moon, and because it is mental in nature, it is a sacrifice belonging to Prajāpati.
"The sacrifice is the mind; one who wears the sacrificial cord (yajñopavītī) should sip water"—thus the teachers are in agreement that this is a constant rule. How is it said [otherwise]?
Thus ends the third chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra.
Now begins the fourth chapter in the second book.

"Whether it be a deer-skin, a garment, or a thread—whatever his second [upper] garment may be—with that he performs the *upavīta* (the sacred thread ceremony). He thereby creates the very mark of a deity," so says the Brāhmaṇa. 1. Then he sips water; this too is the second [act]. He should drink three times with verses containing the word *ap-* (water), and wipe his mouth three times with the *vyāhṛtis*. Or alternatively, he should drink three times with the *vyāhṛtis*, and wipe his mouth three times with verses containing the word *ap-*. By saying, "The gods of the sacrifice, the gods of the gods," he effects a union between the sacrifice and the gods. 2.

Now, regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices, he establishes the connection between the sacrifice and the gods: Āditya is the Adhvaryu, Candramas is the Brahman, Agni is the Hotṛ, Vāyu is the Āgnīdhra; from the Cāturmāsya sacrifices onwards, the Aśvins are the two Adhvaryus, Parjanya is the Udgātṛ, the Waters are the Hotrakas, and the Rays are the Camasādhvaryus.

Then, for the householder, having performed the Vaiśvadeva offering and given the first portion [to the gods], eating at the two appointed times is the human rite. Every month, in the latter fortnight, the monthly rite for the ancestors is performed.
At both times, there is the service of the fire and oblations; every half-month, the Pārvaṇa rite for the gods is performed.

(6) For the three [classes], there are three rules which amount to six; man is indeed ordained as sixfold—therefore, this is the redemption of the self. (7) There are five great sacrifices: the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to the spirits, the sacrifice to men, and the sacrifice to Brahman. (8)
The sacrifice to the gods consists of the utterance of *svāhā* up to the firewood; 9. the sacrifice to the ancestors consists of the utterance of *svadhā* up to the vessel of boiled rice; 10.
the sacrifice to the beings consists of the utterance of *namas* up to the flowers. 11.
The sacrifice to humans (*manuṣyayajña*) consists of giving gifts, starting from roots, fruits, and vegetables.
(12) The sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*) consists of the syllable *oṃ*, starting from the *vyāhṛtis*.

(13) Now, his guests who have arrived—belonging to the various castes and stages of life, who bring blessings, who are worthy of rising for, who are worthy of the guest-offering (*arghya*), who are to be honored, who are intimate, who are confidential, and who are trustworthy—[must be treated with hospitality]. (14)
One who is weary, whom one has never seen before nor heard of, who comes seeking only food and for no other purpose—he becomes a guest (atithi).
Or rather, whoever among all the social classes arrives at the proper time as occasion permits, he becomes the most excellent guest among all guests.

Furthermore, those related by birth to one's mother-in-law or father-in-law may come repeatedly, addressing one with affectionate ties; likewise, those sent on errands also become guests when they arrive.

A friend, a fellow student, a fellow traveler, and Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Rathakāras who possess houses, maintain the sacred fires, and own ox-carts or chariots—these are guests. (18) Having placed those of different social ranks (vipaṅkti) among them, one should offer all desired objects, including oxen and cattle.
(19) It is also known from the Brāhmaṇa: "Therefore, among guests, he who possesses an ox-cart and he who possesses a chariot are most honored; he who knows thus becomes most highly honored. (20)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra.
Now begins the fifth chapter in the second book.
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya should arrive together, the Brāhmaṇa is the guest; [one should offer] consolation to the Kṣatriya. 1.

Now, if a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya should arrive together, the Kṣatriya guest should offer consolation to the Vaiśya. (2) If a Vaiśya and a Śūdra should arrive together, the Vaiśya guest should offer consolation to the Śūdra. (3) If a Śūdra has arrived as a guest, one should employ him in work. (4)

Now, if a student (*brahmacārī*) should come home while traveling on a journey for the sake of his mother, father, or teacher, one should not rise to meet him; rather, having said "Welcome," and having provided a seat and water for washing the feet, one should speak of his welfare and sit near him.
(5) One should give him a *kāpāla* [alms-bowl] and say, "Observe your religious observance (*niyama*) alone.
(6) To one who has returned, they say "Alms-food" (*bhaikṣa*); one should bring food from the very house as the alms-food, and that is the service due to him. (7)
Now, if a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) has arrived, one should say "Welcome," rise to meet him, provide a seat and water for washing the feet, address him with kind words, and attend upon him.
(8) Having ascertained his needs, one should offer him roots, tubers, fruits, vegetables, and wild herbs; this is the service due to him.
(9) Now, if an ascetic (yati) has arrived, one should say "Welcome," rise to meet him, provide a seat and water for washing the feet, address him with kind words, and attend upon him. (10)
One should not address him first, nor should one offer him formal hospitality. (11) At the proper time, however, one should bring food obtained as alms; that is the service due to him.

(12) Now, if he stays there as a guest, having prepared a place for his bed, one should provide light at the proper time; some say there should be no spreading of a seat, while others say one should give it. (13)

A compassionate distribution [of food] is ordained for children, the elderly, women, those who have fallen from their status, and even for those with secret conduct or deformed dress, as well as for dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and so forth.
(14) One who is confused, intoxicated, insane, afflicted, terrified, a king, or a thief—these should be approached with composure in times of emergency.

(15) The teacher, the officiating priest, the father, the maternal uncle, the father-in-law, a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas, an anointed Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya who bestows a thousand [pieces of gold], and the royal chaplain—these are worthy of the *arghya* offering. (16)

The son of one's father’s elder brother, the son of one's younger brother, the son of a teacher, one who knows the *Trimadhu*, one who knows the *Triṇāciketa*, one who knows the *Trisuparṇa*, one who maintains the five fires, one who knows the six Vedāṅgas, one who knows the *Śīrṣaka*, one who knows the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, and those who study the *Atharvāṅgirasa*—these, when they are *snātakas*, are to be honored with massaging, bathing, bedding, ornaments, decorations, and clothing.
(17) Now, if many guests should arrive, among them also the learned, the elderly, the emaciated, and the children are to be honored. (18)

Now, if a guest who is distressed or afflicted by illness should say, "Let this be done for me," one should perform another service even if it is not [otherwise] available. (19) Now, if one does not relinquish the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) that has been prepared for the *Āgrayaṇeṣṭi*, the animal sacrifice, the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, or the *Adhvara* sacrifices, one should give that to him; for it is known from tradition: "The guest is equal to all sacrifices and rituals. (20)

Now, if a guest or a visitor should not eat in someone's house, all the deities become excluded from that person. Therefore, accompanied by his wife and children, he should rise to meet them and offer a seat, water for the feet, a respectful reception, or the arghya offering; he should also bring whatever medicinal herbs are available there. (21) He who attends to guests according to this rule, and he who honors guests according to this rule—neither death, nor affliction, nor failure to return, nor old age, nor sorrow overcomes him; so it is for him who knows this, and for him who knows this. (22)
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra.
Now begins the sixth chapter in the second book:
"As for that which has been stated—that whatever is offered elsewhere than in the sacrificial fire-altar (vihāra) constitutes all the forms of the Pākayajña. 1.

Those very [oblations] which are offered for the purpose of sorcery, purification, pacification, prosperity, or well-being are precisely those that are here described. 2. If a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya should appoint a Brāhmaṇa as his domestic priest (purohita), he should approach him, salute him, and say: "I appoint you for intention, for desire, for success, for immortality, and for life. 4.
The domestic priest mutters: "For his assistance, he [employs] intention; for the fulfillment of his desire, they harness their thoughts to Indra.

(5) He himself mutters: "I place before my mind the divine Intention; may she, the mother of sacrifice, be easy for me to invoke. Whatever I desire with my mind, may that wish be attained—this which is established in my heart.

(6) In all rites dedicated to the gods, the commencement is from the east or the north, and the conclusion is likewise; the procedure is performed from left to right (pradakṣiṇa); the sacrificial cord is worn over the left shoulder; the fires are strewn around with *darbha* grass whose tips point toward the east, or the purification is performed with two strainers whose tips point toward the east or the north. (7)

In the same way, the conclusion of the ritual procedure is reversed for ancestral rites (*pitrya*): the fires are strewn with *darbha* grass whose tips point toward the south, or the purification (*utpavana*) is performed with a strainer whose fringes point toward the south and west. (8) For these [rites], this very same method of disposal applies: the oblation (*homa*) concludes with the *vyāhṛti*s. (9) Other subsidiary oblations (*upahoma*), which manifest the specific features of the ritual action, are arranged separately and depend upon one another. (10)
At that time, the teachers restored the sacrifice through modifications and additions of the mantras in order to prevent its interruption.

(11) Whoever, knowing thus, performs the sacrifice, and whoever, knowing thus, sacrifices with the sacrifice—verily he sacrifices with the whole sacrifice, and he indeed performs the whole sacrifice. (12) Regarding this, there is this verse: "We have reached even the path of the gods, so that we may accomplish what we were able to carry forward. Agni, the knower, shall sacrifice; he is the Hotṛ; he shall arrange the rites and the seasonal offerings. (13)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra.
Now begins the seventh chapter in the second book:
On the sixth day, having bathed, being pure, wearing white garments, and well-adorned.
Having taken sacrificial food and having fed the well-composed Brahmins,
and once they are fully satiated, he should then cause them to pronounce "an auspicious day," and after clasping their hands in reverence, he should salute and bow down to them.
One should cook a *sthālīpāka* offering from a white cow with a white calf;
it should be consecrated by pouring the remnants of the oblation over it eight thousand times while reciting the *Gāyatrī*.
Having both consumed that which was offered, one should perform the ritual recitation (*pratimantraṇa*).
In the final watch of the night, it is prescribed that [the deceased] goes everywhere. 4.
However, on darbha grass with the tips pointing eastward, one should cause him to lie down with his head toward the east;
having mentally recited the Caturhotṛ formulas, the oblation is performed with the syllable *praṇava*. 5.
"Thus begotten, sons are never lost;
they are never lost. 6.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra.

On the sixth day, having bathed and become pure—just as it has been stated regarding whatever [else may apply]—now, if a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya should come together, there should be a second [garment], either a skin or a cloth, and a thread. Now it is indeed said: "The Brāhmaṇa is the single Hotṛ. Now it is indeed said: "The *nivīta* [mode of wearing the sacred thread] belongs to men. Then, from rice and barley. 7.

Now, regarding rice and barley: it is indeed said, "The *nivīta* [mode of wearing the sacred thread] is for human beings. It is also said, "The Brāhmaṇa is the *ekahotṛ* (the single priest). His second [garment] is either a deerskin or a cloth, or a cord. Now, if a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya should come together, [the rule applies] as previously stated, whatever it may be. On the sixth day, having bathed while pure—thus ends the second book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra*.
Thus the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaparibhāṣā* is completed.
